column1: # source: WRITTEN FROM KNOWLEDGE, not extracted from any book or database. Each row is a meaning split (PW-1636, proposal-2026-11-10-paradigms-and-conquest.md Part 2, P2): a loan that comes in for the parent meaning under elite rule or intense trade may be kept beside the native word with the narrower child meaning (the native word keeps the parent). After: Baugh & Cable 2002 (A History of the English Language, 5th ed., ch. 7: ox/beef < OF boef 'ox', swine/pork < porc, sheep/mutton < moton, calf/veal < veel, deer/venison < venesoun 'hunted game'); Durkin 2014 (Borrowed Words: the meat sense is an English specialisation, centuries after the Conquest); Japanese ushi 'cow' beside gyuuniku 'beef'; the Latin product layer of Germanic (vinum > wine, caseus > cheese) for ingredient > product.

# columns: parent = the meaning the donor's word had (an animal, an ingredient); child = the narrower meaning it keeps in the receiver (its meat, the product made from it); kind = meat | product (contact.py: elite and takeover rule split both kinds, trade and mixed cities only products); example = a real case.

# Every meat:<animal> child is also a concept of its own (lexicon._MEAT): a lect without the split names it with a compound of the animal and MEAT (data/compounds.tsv), the global default (German Rindfleisch, Korean sogogi, Mandarin niurou).

column4: English beef < Old French boef 'ox', beside native cow, ox
English pork < Old French porc 'pig', beside native swine
English mutton < Old French moton 'ram, sheep', beside native sheep
English poultry < Old French pouletrie, beside native hen, fowl
English venison < Old French venesoun 'hunted game', beside native deer
Germanic *kasjus 'cheese' < Latin caseus, beside native milk
Latin butyrum < Greek boutyron 'cow-cheese', borrowed into Germanic beside native milk
English flour (the 'flower' of meal) < Old French flor, beside native corn
Swahili mkate, Hausa burodi: the made thing borrowed, the grain kept
Germanic *win < Latin vinum, beside native grape and berry words
English sugar < Arabic sukkar, beside native cane
